prompt: Write a note to a friend about lessons from rebuilding a service people depend on every day. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
Hey Sam,

You asked what I learned from the rewrite, so here it is, while it's still fresh.

First, the boring parts matter most. We spent weeks on the new architecture, but the thing users noticed was whether their saved settings and old links still worked. People don't care that your code is cleaner. They care that Tuesday looks like Monday. We wrote down every behavior the old system had, including the weird ones, and treated each as a promise until proven otherwise. A few "bugs" turned out to be features someone's whole workflow relied on.

Second, don't do a big-bang cutover. We ran old and new side by side and sent a sliver of traffic to the new one, then compared the outputs. The differences were humbling. Every mismatch was either a real bug in the new system or an undocumented quirk in the old one, and we needed to know about both. Rolling back took one config change, and that made everyone braver and calmer.

Third, the old system is a record of every hard lesson the team ever learned. Those ugly special cases exist because something broke once. Before deleting any of them, I asked why it was there. Sometimes nobody remembered, and I kept it anyway until the logs showed it never fired. Deleting from ignorance is how you relearn old outages.

Fourth, tell people early and plainly. We posted what was changing, when, and how to reach us if something broke. The few angry messages we got were mostly from people who'd been surprised, not from people who disliked the change. A short heads-up did more than any amount of polish.

Fifth, watch the team, not just the system. The last 10% of a migration is exhausting and unglamorous. Pace it, celebrate small milestones, and don't let the one person who understands the legacy code carry it alone. We nearly burned someone out, and I'm still annoyed I didn't notice sooner.

Finally, I'd resist the urge to add features during the rewrite. Every new thing makes it harder to tell whether a problem comes from the migration or from the addition. Match behavior first, improve after.

If you're ever doing one of these, call me before you start, not halfway through. I'd happily share the checklist we built. It's rough, but it would have saved us a month.

Talk soon,
[name]
